review_comments.body:
![critical](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/critical.svg)

The content from the RSS feed is being imported and will be rendered as raw HTML because `TopicEmbed.import` sets `cook_method: :raw_html`. However, the content is not sanitized here. This creates a critical Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability, as any malicious script in the RSS feed content will be executed in users' browsers. You must sanitize the content before passing it to `TopicEmbed.import`. You can use the `Sanitize` gem which is already a dependency.

```ruby
        content = Sanitize.fragment(CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub), Sanitize::Config::RELAXED)
```

![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

`ALLOWALL` is not a standard value for the `X-Frame-Options` header and may be ignored by browsers, potentially leaving the page vulnerable to clickjacking. To securely allow embedding on a specific domain, you should use `ALLOW-FROM` with the URI of the embedding site. Since the referer is validated against `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`, you can construct a safe origin from it.

```ruby
      response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOW-FROM #{URI(request.referer).scheme}://#{URI(request.referer).host}"
```

![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

Using `open` from `open-uri` with a URL from site settings can be a security risk. While site settings are admin-controlled, it's still possible to configure a malicious URL (e.g., `file:///etc/passwd` or `|/bin/ls`). This could lead to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) or local file inclusion. It's safer to use a library that strictly handles HTTP/HTTPS requests, such as `HTTParty` or `Net::HTTP`.

![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg) The `url` variable is interpolated directly into an HTML `` tag. If the URL contains malicious content (e.g., a `javascript:` scheme), it could lead to a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability. Although there's a regex check on the URL, it's not sufficient to prevent all attacks. You should always HTML-escape content before inserting it into HTML attributes. ```ruby contents << "\n
\n#{I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{CGI.escapeHTML(url)}")}\n" ```

![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

Using `open` from `open-uri` with a URL that can be influenced by a user (`embed_url` from `TopicRetriever`) is a security risk. It can lead to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), local file inclusion (e.g., `file:///etc/passwd`), or remote command execution (e.g., `|/bin/ls`). It's safer to use a library that strictly handles HTTP/HTTPS requests, such as `HTTParty` or `Net::HTTP`, and validates that the URL scheme is `http` or `https`.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The script assumes an element with the ID `discourse-comments` always exists. If it doesn't, `comments` will be `null` (from line 5) and this line will raise a `TypeError`, breaking the script. It's safer to check for the existence of the `comments` element before trying to append a child to it. For example, by adding `if (!comments) { return; }` after line 5.

Executing this synchronously within the `TopicRetriever`, which can be triggered from a web request via `EmbedController`, may lead to long request times and potential timeouts. This is especially problematic as it runs before checking if the specific URL exists in the feed. Consider refactoring this to be more efficient or to run asynchronously.

The page automatically reloads every 30 seconds. If the background job to retrieve the topic fails repeatedly or takes longer than 30 seconds, this will result in an infinite loop of page reloads. This provides a poor user experience and can put unnecessary load on the server. Many RSS feeds use `description` instead of `content`, or may have items with neither field. When `i.content` is `nil`, calling `.scrub` raises a `NoMethodError`, crashing the scheduled feed polling job.

### Unused `feed_key` method is dead code **Low Severity** The `feed_key` method is defined but never called anywhere in the codebase. While the impact is limited to iframe resize manipulation, this is a weak security pattern.

## Why `open-uri` is risky in Rails
- **SSRF:** attackers can supply URLs that hit internal services (e.g., `http://localhost/`, RFC1918 ranges) or cloud metadata endpoints (notably `169.254.169.254`). - **Protocol/scheme surprises:** `OpenURI` is a convenience wrapper around HTTP/HTTPS and FTP fetching, so if you don’t strictly constrain scheme/host, you’re effectively offering a “fetch any URL” feature. ([docs.ruby-lang.org](https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/3.2/OpenURI.html?utm_source=openai))  
- **Command injection footgun:** `open(...)` can spawn a subprocess if the “path” starts with `|` (this is why scanners like Brakeman warn on `open(params[:url])`). ## What “secure” usually looks like (practical mitigations)
1. **Don’t use `open-uri` on user input.** Use an HTTP client (Net::HTTP/Faraday) and treat the URL as untrusted data. ([stackoverflow.com](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/49280250/brakeman-generates-command-injection-warning-when-using-nokogiri-to-open-an-user?utm_source=openai))  
2. **Allowlist destinations** (best defense): only permit known hosts (and typically only `https`). ([cheatsheetseries.owasp.org](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html?utm_source=openai))

4. **Control redirects**: either disable redirects or re-validate every redirect target (SSRF often “starts” external and redirects internal). ([cheatsheetseries.owasp.org](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html?utm_source=openai))

Without one, Ruby raises a `SyntaxError`. The fix is to change `<%- end if %>` to `<%- end %>`. **Impact:** The `embed#best` action will crash with a SyntaxError every time a topic is found (`@topic_view` is set), completely breaking the embed comments feature.

🔴 **XSS via unescaped `request.referer` in JavaScript string literal** In the embed layout at `app/views/layouts/embed.html.erb:11`, `request.referer` is interpolated into a JavaScript single-quoted string using `<%= %>`. Rails' default HTML escaping does not escape single quotes, so a referer URL containing a `'` character in the path (e.g., `http://eviltrout.com/page'+alert(1)+'`) breaks out of the JS string and enables script injection.
Root Cause The code at line 11: ```erb parent.postMessage({type: 'discourse-resize', height: document['body'].offsetHeight}, '<%= request.referer %>'); ``` The `ensure_embeddable` filter at `app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:26` only validates that the referer's **host** matches `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The path and query components are not sanitized. Since `<%= %>` only HTML-escapes (`<`, `>`, `&`, `"`), a single quote in the URL path passes through unescaped, breaking out of the JavaScript string context. The fix should use `escape_javascript` (or `j`) helper: `'<%= escape_javascript(request.referer) %>'`. **Impact:** An attacker can craft a referer URL with the correct host but a malicious path containing `'` to inject arbitrary JavaScript in the embed iframe context.

Detailed Explanation At `app/models/topic_embed.rb:13`: ```ruby contents << "\n
\n...\n" ``` The `<<` operator modifies the string in place. When `import_remote` (line 52) calls `import` with `doc.content`, the Readability document's content string is permanently modified. `<%- end if %>` generates the Ruby code `end if`, which is a syntax error — the `if` modifier requires a condition expression following it. This will cause a `SyntaxError` when Rails compiles the template, making the `best` embed page entirely non-functional.

  <%- end %>

```

**🚨 issue (security):** Using `default: 1` for `cook_method` makes all existing posts render as raw HTML

`Post.cook_methods` maps `0 => :regular` and `1 => :raw_html`, so setting `default: 1` with `null: false` will make all existing posts be treated as raw HTML and skip the cooking pipeline, introducing a behavior change and XSS risk. Use `default: 0` and/or run a data migration to explicitly set `raw_html` only where intended.

**🚨 issue (security):** Raw HTML embeds are rendered without any sanitization, which is a strong XSS risk

`import` sends remote `contents` through `absolutize_urls` and then creates the post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, completely bypassing the cooking/sanitization pipeline. Since `absolutize_urls` only rewrites `href`/`src` and does not remove dangerous tags/attributes, any `<script>` or `on*` attributes in the feed will execute in the Discourse origin. Please either route this content through the normal cook/sanitization flow (i.e. don’t use `raw_html`) or explicitly sanitize with a restrictive allowlist of tags/attributes before saving, similar to the Readability-based sanitization in `import_remote`.

**🚨 suggestion (security):** `open(url)` is used without timeouts or error handling, which can hang or be abused for SSRF

This can indefinitely block workers on slow/unresponsive hosts and exposes an SSRF vector if `url` is user-controlled. Prefer an HTTP client with explicit timeouts and network restrictions (e.g., block internal IP ranges, limit response size), and handle network errors so a single bad URL doesn’t disrupt processing.

Suggested implementation:

```ruby
  def self.import_remote(user, url, opts=nil)
    require 'ruby-readability'

    opts ||= {}

    begin
      response = Excon.get(
        url,
        connect_timeout: 5,
        read_timeout: 10,
        write_timeout: 5,
        idempotent: true
      )

      return unless response.status == 200

      html = response.body
    rescue Excon::Error, SocketError, StandardError => e
      Rails.logger.warn("TopicEmbed#import_remote failed to fetch URL #{url}: #{e.class} - #{e.message}")
      return
    end

    doc = Readability::Document.new(
      html,
      tags: %w[div p code pre h1 h2 h3 b em i strong a img],
      attributes: %w[href src]
    )

    TopicEmbed.import(user, url, opts[:title] || doc.title, doc.content)
  end

```

To fully address SSRF and resource-exhaustion concerns, you may also want to:

1. **Enforce SSRF checks**: Before calling `Excon.get`, validate `url` using whatever SSRF protection utilities the app already uses (e.g., helpers that reject internal/private IPs, loopback, link-local, etc.).
2. **Limit response size**: If your HTTP stack supports it, cap the maximum number of bytes read from the response (e.g., discard or abort if `response.body` exceeds a configured limit).
3. **Centralize HTTP config**: If the codebase already has a wrapper (e.g., a `HttpClient` or similar) with standard timeouts and proxy/SSL settings, use that instead of calling `Excon.get` directly, to keep behavior consistent across the app.

**issue:** Assuming `i.content` is always present can raise when the feed omits it

`SimpleRSS` may not set `i.content` for all feeds (some only have `description`/`summary`/`content:encoded`), so `i.content.scrub` can raise on `nil`. Consider selecting the first available field (e.g. `i.content || i.description || i.summary`) and handling the case where all are `nil` before unescaping/scrubbing.

### Analysis
• Critical default value bug: cook_method migration sets default to 1 (raw_html) instead of 0 (regular), causing all posts to bypass sanitization by default - immediate logic and security failure that affects both new and existing content after migration.

• Multiple XSS and injection vulnerabilities: Combination of unsanitized raw_html rendering, skip_validations in PostCreator, raw helper in views without sanitization, and inverted origin check in embed.js (line 17: `indexOf() === -1` accepts ANY origin except discourse URL) creates exploitable cross-frame attack vectors and potential RCE chain.

• Unprotected SSRF attack surface: Both TopicEmbed.import_remote and Jobs::PollFeed use open(url) without timeout protections, private network blocking, IP restrictions, or redirect limits - allows attackers to probe internal networks and cloud metadata endpoints.

• Race conditions and missing error handling: TopicEmbed.import has check-then-act pattern vulnerable to duplicate topic creation under concurrent requests; feed parsing lacks defensive nil checks for missing content fields, causing silent job failures.

## What the bug is

In `app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb` at line 35, the code calls `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` on each RSS/ATOM feed item. The problem is that `i.content` returns `nil` when the feed item does not have a `<content>` or `<content:encoded>` element. Calling `.scrub` on `nil` raises `NoMethodError: undefined method scrub for nil:NilClass`.

## Why this commonly occurs

RSS 2.0 feeds typically use `<description>` for item content rather than `<content>`. The RSS 2.0 specification defines `<description>` as the standard element for item body text. Many popular blogs and news sites produce RSS 2.0 feeds with only `<description>`. SimpleRSS (the gem used here) returns `nil` for any element that doesn't exist in the feed, so `i.content` will be `nil` for these feeds while `i.description` would contain the actual content.

## Step-by-step proof

1. An admin configures `feed_polling_url` to point to a standard RSS 2.0 feed (e.g., a WordPress blog feed).
2. The `PollFeed` job runs hourly and calls `poll_feed`.
3. SimpleRSS parses the feed and iterates over items.
4. For a typical RSS 2.0 item like `<item><title>Hello</title><description>Post body</description><link>http://example.com/post</link></item>`, `i.content` returns `nil` because there is no `<content>` element.
5. Line 35 calls `nil.scrub`, which raises `NoMethodError`.
6. The exception propagates up and crashes the entire `PollFeed` job. No subsequent items are processed.

## Impact

Since `sidekiq_options retry: false` is set on line 12, the job will not be retried after failure. The feed polling feature is completely broken for any RSS 2.0 feed that uses `<description>` instead of `<content>`. The job runs hourly, so each hour it will attempt and fail again on the same item, never importing any feed items. This effectively makes the feed polling feature unusable for a large class of common RSS feeds.

Replace line 35 with:
```ruby
raw_content = i.content || i.description
next if raw_content.blank?
content = CGI.unescapeHTML(raw_content.scrub)
```

This falls back to `i.description` when `i.content` is nil, and skips items that have neither field, preventing the `NoMethodError` and allowing the job to continue processing remaining items.

The `postMessageReceived` handler in `embed.js` validates the origin of incoming `postMessage` events using `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`. This is a substring check rather than a strict origin comparison. The check passes if `e.origin` appears anywhere within the `discourseUrl` string.

Consider a Discourse instance with `discourseUrl = "http://discourse.example.com/"`. An attacker controlling the domain `http://discourse.example.co` could send a `postMessage` to the embedding page. The check `"http://discourse.example.com/".indexOf("http://discourse.example.co")` returns `0` (not `-1`), so the origin check passes. ## Step-by-step proof

1. The embedding page loads `embed.js`, which sets `discourseUrl` to something like `"http://discourse.example.com/"`.
2. An attacker registers `discourse.example.co` and hosts a page that opens the embedding page in an iframe or window.

## Why existing code does not prevent it

The `indexOf` method checks for substring containment, not origin equality. There is no URL parsing or strict comparison happening, so any origin that happens to be a prefix or substring of the discourse URL will bypass the check.

## Impact

The impact is minimal. The only action the handler performs after the origin check is setting `iframe.height`. An attacker who bypasses this check can only manipulate the iframe height on the embedding page, which is a cosmetic UI issue. There is no data exfiltration, code execution, or other security-sensitive behavior exposed.

Replace the substring check with a strict origin comparison:

golden_comments.comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.

You have defined the `self.downsize` method twice in this file. In Ruby, the last definition of a method overwrites any previous ones. This means the `downsize` method that accepts `max_width` and `max_height` (lines 145-147) will be overwritten by this new definition that accepts a `dimensions` string. This is a critical breaking change and will likely cause errors in other parts of the application that call `downsize` with separate width and height arguments.

To fix this, you should rename this new method to avoid the conflict, for example to `downsize_by_dimension_string`.

![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

Hardcoding `maxSizeKB` to `10 * 1024` (10MB) here, and similarly on line 246, ignores the site settings for maximum file size. This will lead to a confusing user experience where the client-side validation allows a file that might be rejected or unexpectedly downsized by the server if the site settings are configured to a smaller size. The client-side limit should remain synchronized with the server-side settings. Please revert to using the site setting.

```suggestion
    var maxSizeKB = Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'];
```

![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

The maximum download size for a URL is hardcoded to `10.megabytes`. This should be a configurable setting rather than a magic number to allow administrators to control this limit. This is related to the hardcoded values in the JavaScript files. It would be better to use a site setting. Please revert to using `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` or introduce a new, specific site setting if a larger limit is required for downsizing.

```ruby
        tempfile = FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, "discourse-upload-#{type}") rescue nil
```

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The number of downsizing attempts (`5` on line 65) and the downsizing percentage (`"80%"` on line 67) are hardcoded. These magic values should be extracted into well-named constants at the top of the class, or ideally, be made into configurable site settings to provide more flexibility and improve maintainability.

## Code Review

This pull request introduces a feature to automatically downsize large images upon upload. While this is a valuable addition, the current implementation has a few issues. There are hardcoded size limits on both the client and server-side, which override configurable site settings and could lead to inconsistent behavior. The downsizing logic also contains magic numbers for retry attempts and resizing percentages, which should be made configurable for better maintainability. Most importantly, there is a critical bug in `app/models/optimized_image.rb` where a method is redefined, which will break existing functionality.

SSRF/Resource exhaustion:
`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` increases the allowable fetch size for user-provided URLs in the API path, which can amplify SSRF impact and bandwidth/CPU usage. Ensure `FileHelper.download` enforces allowlists/denylists for internal IP ranges, redirects, and schemes, and consider aligning the limit with site settings or adding stricter controls for remote URL uploads.
⚡ Recommended focus areas for review

Possible Issue `downsize` is defined twice with different signatures; in Ruby the later method definition overwrites the earlier one. This likely breaks callers expecting the `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` variant and may cause runtime errors or incorrect downsizing behavior. Consider consolidating into a single method (e.g., one that accepts either a dimensions string or width/height) or renaming one of them. ```ruby def self.resize(from, to, width, height, opts={}) optimize("resize", from, to, "#{width}x#{height}", opts) end def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) optimize("downsize", from, to, "#{max_width}x#{max_height}", opts) end def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}) optimize("downsize", from, to, dimensions, opts) end def self.optimize(operation, from, to, dimensions, opts={}) method_name = "#{operation}_instructions" method_name += "_animated" if !!opts[:allow_animation] && from =~ /\.GIF$/i instructions = self.send(method_name.to_sym, from, to, dimensions, opts) convert_with(instructions, to) end ```
Logic/Config Mismatch The server now downloads API-provided URLs with a hard 10MB limit but then attempts to downsize to meet `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. If `max_image_size_kb` is smaller than 10MB, the initial download can exceed the configured limit (and if it’s larger, downloads will be capped unexpectedly). Also, the downsizing call passes `"80%"` as the dimensions argument, which may not match what `downsize_instructions` expects (typically `WxH`), so validate that this actually reduces file size. ```ruby tempfile = FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, "discourse-upload-#{type}") rescue nil filename = File.basename(URI.parse(url).path) else tempfile = file.tempfile filename = file.original_filename content_type = file.content_type end # allow users to upload large images that will be automatically reduced to allowed size if tempfile && tempfile.size > 0 && SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb > 0 && FileHelper.is_image?(filename) attempt = 5 while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails) attempt -= 1 end end ```
UX Inconsistency Client-side upload size checks and 413 messaging are now hard-coded to 10MB, ignoring site settings (previously `max_*_size_kb` / `max_image_size_kb`). This can cause confusing behavior where the browser blocks uploads that the server would accept (or vice versa). Consider deriving the max from `Discourse.SiteSettings` (or a server-provided constant) and keeping it consistent with the server download/processing limits. ```javascript // check file size var fileSizeKB = file.size / 1024; var maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024; // 10MB if (fileSizeKB > maxSizeKB) { bootbox.alert(I18n.t('post.errors.file_too_large', { max_size_kb: maxSizeKB })); return false; ```

### Duplicate method definition breaks existing callers **High Severity** Two `downsize` methods are defined with the same name—one taking `max_width, max_height` arguments (line 145) and another taking a single `dimensions` argument (line 149). In Ruby, the second definition overwrites the first. The existing caller in `resize_emoji.rb` uses `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)` with 4 positional arguments, which will now fail with an `ArgumentError` since only the 3-argument version exists.
Additional Locations (1) - [`app/models/optimized_image.rb#L144-L146`](https://github.com/code-review-benchmark/discourse__discourse-graphite__bugbot__PR1__20260122/blob/ffbaf8c54269df2ce510de91245760fddce09896/app/models/optimized_image.rb#L144-L146)

### Client-side validation ignores attachment size limit setting **Medium Severity** The client-side file size validation now uses a hardcoded 10MB limit for all file types instead of the type-specific `max_{type}_size_kb` site setting. While this works for images (which get auto-downsized server-side), attachments have no such downsizing. Users can select attachments larger than `max_attachment_size_kb`, the client accepts them, but the server rejects them during upload validation. This creates a confusing experience where files pass client validation but fail after upload.

### Animated GIFs lose animation during auto-downsize **Medium Severity** The auto-downsize code passes `tempfile.path` to `OptimizedImage.downsize`, but `tempfile.path` is a system-generated path without the original file extension (e.g., `/tmp/RackMultipart...`). The animated GIF detection in `optimize()` relies on matching the path against `/\.GIF$/i`, which will never match. As a result, animated GIFs are processed with `downsize_instructions` which uses `[0]` to extract only the first frame, permanently destroying all animation frames.

The URL-download size cap is now hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings (e.g. `max_image_size_kb` / `max_attachment_size_kb`). This changes behavior for API URL uploads: the app may download significantly larger files than admins configured, increasing bandwidth/CPU risk.

Consider deriving the download cap from the relevant site setting (or limiting to 10MB only for images while respecting `max_attachment_size_kb` for non-images).

The downsize loop ignores the return value from `OptimizedImage.downsize`. If the conversion fails, this will retry up to 5 times without making progress and still proceed to `Upload.create_for`, which will then reject the file as too large.

Consider breaking early (and/or returning an error) when `downsize` returns false, and optionally logging the failure to aid debugging.
```suggestion
          success = OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)
          unless success
            Rails.logger.warn("Failed to downsize upload #{filename.inspect} on attempt #{6 - attempt}")
            break
          end
```

There are existing controller specs for uploads (`spec/controllers/uploads_controller_spec.rb`), but no coverage for the newly introduced behavior of accepting an oversized image and automatically downsizing it below `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`.

Please add a spec that uploads an image larger than `max_image_size_kb` (but under the new cap) and asserts the upload succeeds and the stored filesize is within the configured limit.

`downsize` is defined twice. In Ruby the later definition overrides the earlier one, so calls expecting the `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` signature (e.g. `app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb`) will now pass the wrong arguments into `optimize`, likely raising at `opts[:allow_animation]`.

Consider keeping a single `downsize` method that is backwards-compatible (e.g. accept either a geometry string or width/height) or rename the new geometry-string variant so existing callers remain valid.

This change alters `downsize`/`optimize` argument conventions (width/height → geometry string). There are existing specs for `OptimizedImage` (e.g. `spec/models/optimized_image_spec.rb`), but none appear to cover `downsize` invocation paths.

Please add/adjust tests to cover both the legacy `downsize(path, path, w, h, opts)` call pattern and the new geometry-string usage so future refactors don’t silently break callers.

## Pull request overview Adds support for accepting larger image uploads and automatically downsizing them to fit the configured maximum image size. **Changes:** - Updated `OptimizedImage` resizing/downsize plumbing to pass ImageMagick “geometry” strings through the pipeline. - Added a server-side loop in `UploadsController#create_upload` to repeatedly downsize oversized images before creating an `Upload`. - Changed client-side upload size checks (and API URL download cap) to a hardcoded 10MB limit. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 3 out of 3 changed files in this pull request and generated 6 comments. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | app/models/optimized_image.rb | Refactors resize/downsize plumbing to use geometry strings; introduces a new `downsize` signature. | | app/controllers/uploads_controller.rb | Attempts to accept oversized images and downsize them before `Upload.create_for`; increases API URL download cap. | | app/assets/javascripts/discourse/lib/utilities.js | Hardcodes client-side file size limits and 413 messaging to 10MB. |

**`tempfile.size` returns stale size after in-place ImageMagick conversion**

## What the bug is

The original code on line 182 used `Discourse.SiteSettings["max_" + type + "_size_kb"]` to dynamically look up the correct size limit based on the upload type. When `type` is `"image"`, it resolves to `max_image_size_kb`; when `type` is `"attachment"`, it resolves to `max_attachment_size_kb`. The PR replaces this with a flat `10 * 1024` (10MB) for all upload types.

## Why it matters for attachments

The server-side auto-downsizing logic added in `uploads_controller.rb` (lines 63-68) only applies to images — it checks `FileHelper.is_image?(filename)` before attempting to downsize. Non-image attachments (PDFs, zip files, documents, etc.) pass through with no modification. So while the 10MB client-side limit is justified for images (the server will shrink them down), it is not justified for attachments.

## Step-by-step proof

1. Admin configures `max_attachment_size_kb = 3072` (3MB) and `max_image_size_kb = 1024` (1MB).
2. A user attempts to upload a 5MB PDF file.
3. In `validateUploadedFiles` (line 161), `type` is set to `"attachment"` because `isAnImage` returns false for `.pdf`.
4. `validateUploadedFile` is called with `type = "attachment"`.

The existing caller in `app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)` with 5 arguments, which will raise `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (given 5, expected 3..4)` at runtime, breaking emoji resizing. The old 4-arg `downsize` on line 145-147 should be removed.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## The Bug

The PR adds a new 3-argument `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` method at line 149 to support the new percentage-based downsizing call in `uploads_controller.rb` (e.g., `downsize(path, path, "80%")`). However, the original 4-argument `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 was not removed.

## Why This Is a Problem

In Ruby, method dispatch is based solely on method name, not arity. When two methods share the same name, the last definition completely replaces the first. This means the 4-argument version at line 145 is dead code — it can never be called. Only the 3-argument version at line 149 exists at runtime.

## Step-by-Step Proof

1. `app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14` calls: `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)` — that is 5 positional arguments.
2. The only surviving `downsize` method signature is `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`, which accepts 3 required args + 1 optional keyword-style arg = 3 to 4 arguments total.
3. Ruby will attempt to match 5 arguments against the (from, to, dimensions, opts={}) signature. Since `opts={}` can absorb at most 1 extra argument, the maximum accepted is 4. With 5 arguments, Ruby raises: `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (given 5, expected 3..4)`.

## Impact

This will break emoji resizing entirely. Any time `resize_emoji.rb` runs (which happens when custom emoji are uploaded), it will crash with an ArgumentError. This is a runtime error that would not be caught without actually triggering the code path.

## How to Fix

Remove the dead 4-arg `downsize` method (lines 145-147). The existing caller in `resize_emoji.rb` should be updated to use the new dimensions string format: `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, "100x100", opts)`. This aligns with how `resize` was already updated on line 142 to construct the dimensions string inline.

🔴 Animated GIF downsizing is broken for all upload paths. For regular browser uploads, Rack tempfile paths lack a `.gif` extension, so the `from =~ /\.GIF$/i` check in `optimize()` never matches and `convert` with `[0]` strips the animation. For API URL uploads where the extension is preserved, gifsicle is triggered but `--resize-fit 80%` is invalid syntax (gifsicle requires WxH pixel dimensions, not percentages), so it fails silently. The `allow_animation` option is effectively dead code.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## Bug Analysis

The new downsize loop at `uploads_controller.rb:67` calls:
```ruby
OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)
```
This passes `"80%"` as the dimensions string and `allow_animation` to preserve animated GIF handling. However, animated GIF preservation is broken through two independent failure modes that cover all upload paths.

## Failure Mode 1: Regular Browser Uploads

When a user uploads a file through the browser, `file.tempfile` is a Rack tempfile with a path like `/tmp/RackMultipart20160101-1234-abcdef` — no file extension. In `optimize()` at `optimized_image.rb:155`, the animation detection check is:
```ruby
method_name += "_animated" if !!opts[:allow_animation] && from =~ /\.GIF$/i
```
Since the Rack tempfile path does not end in `.gif`, this regex never matches. The code falls through to the non-animated `downsize_instructions`, which builds a `convert` command using `#{from}[0]`. The `[0]` suffix tells ImageMagick to only process the first frame, stripping all animation from the GIF.

## Failure Mode 2: API URL Uploads

When uploading via the API with a URL (e.g., `https://example.com/image.gif`), `FileHelper.download` at `file_helper.rb:13-14` creates a Tempfile that preserves the URL extension:
```ruby
extension = File.extname(uri.path)
tmp = Tempfile.new([tmp_file_name, extension])
```
So the tempfile path ends in `.gif`, the regex matches, and `downsize_instructions_animated` is called. This delegates to `resize_instructions_animated` which builds:
```
gifsicle input.gif --colors=256 --resize-fit 80% --optimize=3 --output output.gif
```
However, gifsicle does **not** support percentage-based resize — it requires pixel dimensions in `WxH` format (e.g., `640x480`). This causes gifsicle to fail with a non-zero exit status. `convert_with` catches the failure and returns `false`, so the while loop iterates all 5 times doing nothing useful, and the upload proceeds at its original (too-large) size.

## Step-by-Step Proof (API Upload Path)

1. User uploads a GIF via API with URL `https://example.com/large-animation.gif`
2. `FileHelper.download` creates tempfile at e.g. `/tmp/discourse-upload-image20160101-1234-abc.gif`
3. The file exceeds `max_image_size_kb`, so the downsize loop begins
4. `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, "80%", allow_animation: true)` is called
5. In `optimize()`, `from =~ /\.GIF$/i` matches the `.gif` extension → animated path selected
6. `downsize_instructions_animated` → `resize_instructions_animated` builds `gifsicle ... --resize-fit 80% ...`
7. gifsicle fails (invalid percentage syntax) → `convert_with` returns `false`
8. Loop repeats 4 more times, each failing identically
9. Upload proceeds at original oversized dimensions

## Impact

The `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` parameter is completely dead code — animated GIFs will always lose their animation during downsizing (browser uploads) or fail to downsize at all (API uploads). Note that the `.GIF` extension check pattern in `optimize()` is pre-existing (it existed before this PR), but the "80%" percentage issue and the interaction with the new downsize loop are introduced by this PR.

## Fix

Two changes are needed:
1. **Use pixel dimensions instead of percentages**: Calculate the target dimensions from the original image size (e.g., read dimensions with `identify`, compute 80% of each, pass `"WxH"` format)
2. **Pass the original filename or detect MIME type**: Instead of relying on the tempfile path extension, check the file content type or pass the original filename to `optimize()` so the GIF detection works for all upload paths

</details>

### 1. Nil Safety Issue in unsubscribe Action
**File:** `/app/controllers/topics_controller.rb`, lines 105-113

**Description:** The `unsubscribe` action calls `TopicUser.find_by()` and then directly accesses properties on the result without checking for nil. If a user visits the unsubscribe link but doesn't have a TopicUser record (which is possible if they've never interacted with the topic beyond receiving the email), this will raise a `NoMethodError`.

**Historical Context:** 
- The codebase has an established pattern of checking for nil after `find_by` calls. See `app/controllers/badges_controller.rb:35-38` where a similar pattern uses `if user_badge && user_badge.notification` before accessing attributes.
- The existing `set_notifications` action (line 332) uses `TopicUser.change()` method which handles the nil case automatically by creating a new TopicUser record if one doesn't exist (see `app/models/topic_user.rb:77-118`).
- The PR diverges from this established pattern by using `find_by` + direct attribute access instead of using the safer `TopicUser.change()` method.

**Recommended Fix:** Use `TopicUser.change()` instead of `find_by` + `save!`, following the pattern in the `set_notifications` action:

```ruby
def unsubscribe
  @topic_view = TopicView.new(params[:topic_id], current_user)
  
  if slugs_do_not_match || (!request.format.json? && params[:slug].blank?)
    return redirect_to @topic_view.topic.unsubscribe_url, status: 301
  end
  
  tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])
  
  new_level = if tu && tu.notification_level > TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]
    TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]
  else
    TopicUser.notification_levels[:muted]
  end
  
  TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: new_level)
  
  perform_show_response
end
```

**File:** `/lib/email/message_builder.rb`, line 107

**Description:** The PR adds `unsubscribe_url` parameter to the email options (see `app/mailers/user_notifications.rb:295`) but never actually uses it. The `List-Unsubscribe` header continues to point to the user preferences URL instead of the per-topic unsubscribe URL.

**Historical Context:**
- The `List-Unsubscribe` header was introduced in commit 8acdc18bc (Jun 2013) and has always pointed to `user_preferences_url`.
- The PR's stated goal is to provide a "per-topic unsubscribe option" but the RFC 2369 `List-Unsubscribe` header (which many email clients use for their "Unsubscribe" button) still points to the global preferences page.
- The spec test was updated to pass `unsubscribe_url` (line 172) but doesn't verify that this URL is actually used in the header.

**Recommended Fix:** Update the `List-Unsubscribe` header to use the per-topic unsubscribe URL when provided:

**Nil `TopicUser` causes crash**

`TopicUser.find_by` returns `nil` when no record exists for the user/topic combination (e.g., the user received the email but was never explicitly tracked or watched). Calling `.notification_level` on a `nil` reference will raise `NoMethodError: undefined method 'notification_level' for nil:NilClass`, crashing the unsubscribe flow for those users.

```suggestion
    tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])

    if tu.nil?
      TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: TopicUser.notification_levels[:muted])
    elsif tu.notification_level > TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular]
      tu.update!(notification_level: TopicUser.notification_levels[:regular])
    else
      tu.update!(notification_level: TopicUser.notification_levels[:muted])
    end
```

**State mutation on a GET request**

The `unsubscribe` action immediately and silently changes the user's notification level on a GET request, before presenting any UI. Email clients, browser prefetching, link-preview crawlers, or an accidental click can all trigger an irreversible state change. The conventional approach for unsubscribe-via-GET is to show a confirmation page (the frontend `topic-unsubscribe` route already does this) and perform the actual mutation only in response to a subsequent POST/form submission. As implemented, the backend permanently changes the level _before_ the frontend ever renders its notification-options picker, leaving the user without context or confirmation.

**Potential XSS via unescaped triple-mustache** `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` renders its output as raw HTML without escaping. The string is built by interpolating `model.fancyTitle` (user-provided topic title) directly into the locale string `"You will stop receiving notifications for {{title}}."` via `I18n.t`. If `fancyTitle` contains any HTML (e.g. ``), it will be injected into the DOM unescaped. Consider using Ember's `Ember.String.htmlSafe` with explicit escaping of the title value before interpolation, or restructure the template to keep the dynamic title separate from the static HTML tags so double-mustache `{{…}}` can be used safely.

🔴 The `unsubscribe` action requires `ensure_logged_in` (line 28), but the unsubscribe URL is embedded in notification emails for users to click directly. When a logged-out user clicks this link, the `Discourse::NotLoggedIn` exception is caught by `application_controller.rb:97-104`, which silently redirects GET requests to `"/"` (the homepage) with no error message and no unsubscribe action taken. This makes the per-topic email unsubscribe feature non-functional for the most common case: users clicking the link from their email client while not logged in. Consider using a token-based approach similar to the existing `email/unsubscribe/:key` system.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## Bug Analysis

The new `unsubscribe` action in `TopicsController` is added to the `ensure_logged_in` filter list at line 28. This action is specifically designed to be reached via links in notification emails (the `unsubscribe_url` is passed through `user_notifications.rb` and rendered in `notification.html.erb` via the `unsubscribe_link` i18n string). The fundamental problem is that email links are clicked by users who are very often not logged into the forum in their browser.

## Code Path for Logged-Out Users

When a logged-out user clicks the unsubscribe link from an email:
1. The request hits `TopicsController#unsubscribe`
2. Before the action runs, the `ensure_logged_in` before_filter fires (`application_controller.rb:408-410`)
3. Since `current_user` is nil, it raises `Discourse::NotLoggedIn`
4. The `rescue_from Discourse::NotLoggedIn` handler at `application_controller.rb:97-104` catches this
5. Since the request is a GET request (not JSON, not XHR), execution falls to line 103: `redirect_to path("/")`
6. The user is silently redirected to the homepage with **no feedback whatsoever**

## Why This Is Not "Standard Discourse Behavior"

One verifier argued this is intentional because Discourse redirects to login and then back. However, that is **not** what happens here. Reading lines 97-104 of `application_controller.rb`, the handler for `NotLoggedIn` on GET HTML requests does `redirect_to path("/")` — a plain redirect to the homepage root, not to a login page with a return URL. The user sees the homepage with no indication that they needed to log in or that their unsubscribe attempt failed. There is no redirect-back-after-login mechanism in this code path.

## Concrete Example

1. User Alice receives a notification email for topic "Release Notes v2.0" (topic_id: 42)
2. The email contains a link: `https://forum.example.com/t/release-notes-v2-0/42/unsubscribe`

This effectively makes the entire per-topic unsubscribe feature non-functional for the primary use case it was designed for. The existing Discourse email unsubscribe system (`email/unsubscribe/:key` at `config/routes.rb`) uses a unique token-based approach that works without authentication, specifically because email links must work without a login session. The new per-topic unsubscribe should follow the same pattern.

Either: (a) Generate a unique unsubscribe token per user/topic and use token-based authentication similar to `EmailController#unsubscribe`, or (b) at minimum, redirect to a login page with a return URL so the user can authenticate and then be redirected back to complete the unsubscribe action.

## What the bug is

The `unsubscribe_link` translation in `config/locales/server.en.yml` was changed from a single line referencing only `%{user_preferences_url}` to a multi-line string that also references `%{unsubscribe_url}`:

```yaml
unsubscribe_link: |
  To unsubscribe from these emails, visit your [user preferences](%{user_preferences_url}).
  To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, [click here](%{unsubscribe_url}).
```

This introduces a new mandatory interpolation variable that was not previously required.

## The code path

In `lib/email/message_builder.rb`, both `html_part` (line 68) and `body` (line 88) call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` when `add_unsubscribe_link: true` is set. The `template_args` hash is initialized with only `site_name`, `base_url`, and `user_preferences_url`, then merged with `@opts`. The `unsubscribe_url` key only appears in `template_args` if the caller explicitly passes it in `@opts`.

## Why existing code doesn't prevent it

The only current production caller that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` is `send_notification_email` in `app/mailers/user_notifications.rb` (line 294), which was updated in this PR to also pass `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url`. The test spec was similarly updated to pass `unsubscribe_url`. However, `Email::MessageBuilder` is a shared utility class -- there is no guard, default value, or documentation requiring callers to provide `unsubscribe_url`.

## Step-by-step proof

1. A Discourse plugin calls `build_email(user.email, body: 'hello', add_unsubscribe_link: true)` -- this was valid before this PR.
2. `MessageBuilder` initializes `@template_args` as `{site_name: ..., base_url: ..., user_preferences_url: ...}` merged with opts. No `unsubscribe_url` key is present.
3. In `body`, `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` is called.
4. The translation expects `%{unsubscribe_url}` but the key is missing from `template_args`.
5. Ruby I18n raises `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` (or renders `%{unsubscribe_url}` literally depending on I18n exception handler config), breaking the email.

## Impact

This is a breaking change to the `Email::MessageBuilder` public API. Any Discourse plugin that previously used `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without passing `unsubscribe_url` will fail after this change. The core codebase itself is not affected since the only internal caller was updated.

## Fix

Add a default value for `unsubscribe_url` in the `@template_args` initialization in `message_builder.rb`, e.g., defaulting to `user_preferences_url`. Alternatively, the translation could use `%{unsubscribe_url}` with a conditional or be split into two separate translation keys.

</details>

🟡 **Prisma `updateMany` with empty data does not trigger `@updatedAt`, making the call a no-op** The call `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` at `CalendarService.ts:1024` is intended to touch `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` (as stated in the comment on line 1023), but **Prisma's `@updatedAt` decorator is not triggered by `updateMany`** — it only auto-updates on `update` and `upsert` operations.
Root cause and impact From Prisma's documentation: "`updateMany()` does not update `@updatedAt` fields. If you use `@updatedAt`, you should update the field value manually." Since the `data` argument is an empty object `{}`, Prisma generates a query that updates zero columns. The `@updatedAt` field on `SelectedCalendar` (`packages/prisma/schema.prisma` line ~274: `updatedAt DateTime? @updatedAt`) will not be set to the current time. The `updateManyByCredentialId` method at `packages/lib/server/repository/selectedCalendar.ts:400-404` passes the empty data straight through to `prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany({ where: { credentialId }, data: {} })`, which is effectively a no-op. The `UserWithCalendars` type was updated (`packages/lib/getConnectedDestinationCalendars.ts:22-28`) to include `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId`, and the user session query (`packages/lib/server/repository/user.ts:899-900`) now selects these fields, indicating they were intended to be populated. Since `updateMany` never actually touches `updatedAt`, these values will only reflect the record creation time, not the last cache refresh time. **Impact:** `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is never updated after cache refresh, so any downstream consumer relying on it will see stale timestamps. The primary UI cache display currently sources from `CalendarCache.updatedAt` (which works), so the user-visible impact is limited, but the intent of the code is not achieved.

Root cause and impact The intended pattern in this codebase is to use `CalendarCache.init(calendar)` (see `packages/features/calendar-cache/calendar-cache.ts:22-28`) which checks whether the `calendar-cache` feature is globally enabled. When disabled, it returns a `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` whose `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds()` returns `[]`. By directly constructing `new CalendarCacheRepository()`, the handler always queries the database for cache status, even when the feature is turned off. P3: The migration uses `DEFAULT NOW()` which evaluates to the timestamp at migration time for existing rows, but in PostgreSQL `NOW()` as a column default actually evaluates per-row at insert time, so new inserts are fine. However, the migration comment says 'Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty' — yet the SQL does add a default. The real issue is that the Prisma schema uses `@default(now()) @updatedAt` together. The `@updatedAt` directive makes Prisma set the value on every update, but `@default(now())` combined with `@updatedAt` means Prisma will ignore the DB default on creates and use its own `now()`. For raw SQL inserts (which the codebase uses — see `upsertCachedAvailability` using `$queryRaw`), the `@updatedAt` directive won't fire, so `updatedAt` will remain at the DB default `NOW()` from insert time and never get updated by raw queries.

The `@updatedAt` directive makes Prisma set the value on every update, but `@default(now())` combined with `@updatedAt` means Prisma will ignore the DB default on creates and use its own `now()`. For raw SQL inserts (which the codebase uses — see `upsertCachedAvailability` using `$queryRaw`), the `@updatedAt` directive won't fire, so `updatedAt` will remain at the DB default `NOW()` from insert time and never get updated by raw queries.</comment>
```

### Working hours check uses wrong variable for slot end **High Severity** The `end` variable is incorrectly computed using `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`. Both `start` and `end` now have the same value, so the check `end > workingHour.endTime` doesn't actually verify if the slot *ends* after working hours. This allows slots that start within working hours but extend past them to be incorrectly marked as available.

### Dayjs object comparison using === always returns false **Medium Severity** The comparison `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` uses `===` to compare two Dayjs objects. In JavaScript, this compares object references, not values, so it always returns `false`. The comparison needs to use `.isSame()` method, as done correctly on line 119.

### Working hours check uses wrong algorithm for multiple blocks **Medium Severity** The working hours check uses `.find()` to return false (unavailable) when a slot is outside ANY working hour block. The correct logic requires checking if the slot is outside ALL blocks. For users with multiple blocks on the same day (e.g., 9am-12pm and 2pm-6pm), a valid 10am slot would be incorrectly rejected when checked against the 2pm-6pm block, even though it falls within the 9am-12pm block.

🔴 Two bugs in the date override boundary check in `checkIfIsAvailable` (lines 114-123): (1) Line 114 uses `===` to compare two dayjs objects, which is reference equality and will always be `false` -- zero-length overrides (blocked days) are never detected. Use `.isSame()` instead. (2) Line 123 uses strict `isAfter` for the end boundary but the start boundary (lines 117-120) uses `isBefore || isSame`; a slot starting exactly at the override end time passes the check and is incorrectly marked available. Add `|| slotStartTime.isSame(...)` to line 123 for consistency.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## Bug 1: Reference equality on dayjs objects (line 114)

Line 114 compares two dayjs objects using `===`:

```js
if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))
```

In JavaScript, `===` between objects is reference equality, not value equality. Each `dayjs()` call creates a new object, so this comparison will **always** return `false`, even when the underlying timestamps are identical. This is intended to detect zero-length date overrides (where start equals end), which typically represent a day marked as unavailable/blocked.

**Step-by-step proof:** Suppose a user creates a date override with `start = end = 2024-01-15T00:00:00Z` to block the entire day. When `checkIfIsAvailable` runs:
1. `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` creates Object A
2. `dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` creates Object B
3. `Object A === Object B` evaluates to `false` (different references, even though they represent the same time)
4. The code falls through to the `isBefore`/`isAfter` checks, which also don't catch this case (a slot spanning the override point is neither fully before nor fully after it)
5. The `find()` callback returns `undefined` (falsy), so the slot passes the override check
6. `dateOverrideExist` is `true`, so the function returns `true` (available)
7. The slot is incorrectly shown as bookable on a day the user explicitly blocked

The fix is straightforward -- use `.isSame()` instead of `===`:
```js
if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))) {
```

## Bug 2: Asymmetric end boundary check (line 123)

The start boundary check (lines 117-120) correctly uses `isBefore || isSame` (equivalent to `<=`), but the end boundary check (line 123) only uses `isAfter` (equivalent to `>`) without `isSame`. This means a slot whose start time **exactly equals** the override end time is not considered outside the override.

**Step-by-step proof:** Consider a round-robin event where a fixed host has a date override from 08:30-12:30 UTC. Another round-robin host has working hours extending past 12:30, so slot generation produces a 12:30 UTC slot.
1. `slotStartTime` = 12:30 UTC, override end = 12:30 UTC
2. `slotStartTime.isAfter(overrideEnd)` evaluates to `12:30.isAfter(12:30)` which is `false`
3. The `find()` callback returns `undefined`, so the slot is not flagged as outside the override
4. Since `dateOverrideExist` is `true`, the function returns `true` (available)
5. But the slot runs from 12:30 to 13:30 -- entirely **outside** the host's 08:30-12:30 availability window
6. The fixed host is incorrectly considered available for this slot

The fix: add `|| slotStartTime.isSame(...)` to line 123 to match the symmetry of the start boundary check:
```js
if (slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")) || slotStartTime.isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))) {
```

Both bugs are in new code introduced by this PR. The first bug (reference equality) is the more impactful one as it completely breaks zero-length override detection. The second is a boundary edge case that primarily affects round-robin events where slot generation is based on aggregate working hours.

## Bug Description

Lines 141-142 in `checkIfIsAvailable` both compute their value from `slotStartTime`:

```ts

const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();
```

The `end` variable on line 142 should use `slotEndTime` (which is already computed on line 99 as `time.add(eventLength, "minutes").utc()`) instead of `slotStartTime`. As written, `start` and `end` are always identical.

The `checkIfIsAvailable` function is called in multiple places throughout `getSchedule` — for fixed hosts (line 489), loose/round-robin hosts (line 514), and selected slots filtering (line 576). In each case, `workingHours` from the user’s schedule is passed in. The working hours check at lines 138-148 is meant to reject slots that fall outside working hours, but because `end === start`, the check `end > workingHour.endTime` is equivalent to `start > workingHour.endTime`.

## Step-by-Step Proof

Consider a 60-minute event type with working hours from 9:00 (540 minutes) to 17:00 (1020 minutes):

1. A slot at 16:30 UTC is checked: `slotStartTime` = 16:30, `slotEndTime` = 17:30
2. `start` = 16*60 + 30 = 990
3. `end` = 16*60 + 30 = 990 (bug — should be 17*60 + 30 = 1050)
4. Check: `start < 540` → false. `end > 1020` → 990 > 1020 → false
5. The slot passes the working hours check even though it extends 30 minutes past the end of working hours

With the fix (`end = slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()` = 1050), `end > 1020` → true, and the slot would correctly be rejected.

This allows booking slots that start within working hours but extend past them. For longer event types (60, 90, 120 minutes), this could result in bookings being offered well past the organizer’s configured working hours end time.

Line 142 should be:

🔴 When a slot falls within a date override window, `checkIfIsAvailable` returns `true` at line 134 without checking the `busy` array, allowing double bookings during date override periods. For example, a user with a date override from 10am-6pm and an existing booking at 2pm will still show 2pm as available. The fix: remove the early `return true` at line 134 and let execution fall through to the `busy.every()` check at line 153.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## Bug Analysis

The `checkIfIsAvailable` function in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts` has a logic flaw in how it handles date overrides. The function is supposed to determine whether a given time slot is available for booking, considering both date overrides (special availability windows) and existing bookings (busy times). However, the current implementation skips busy-time validation entirely when a slot falls within a date override.

## Code Path

The `dateOverrides.find()` callback (lines 106-127) sets `dateOverrideExist = true` whenever the override is on the same day as the slot (line 113). It then checks if the slot is **outside** the override window — returning `true` from the callback if the slot ends before the override starts, or starts after the override ends. When `find()` returns a truthy result (slot is outside the override), the function correctly returns `false` (unavailable).

The problem occurs when the slot is **within** the override window. In this case, none of the boundary checks trigger, the callback returns `undefined` for that element, and `find()` returns `undefined` (no match found). Execution falls through to line 133-134: `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }`. This immediately returns `true` (available), completely bypassing the `busy.every()` check at line 153.

## Step-by-Step Proof

Consider a user with:
- A date override on March 15 from 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM UTC
- An existing confirmed booking on March 15 from 2:00 PM to 3:00 PM UTC

When checking the 2:00 PM slot:
1. `dateOverrides.find()` iterates over the override for March 15
2. The override date matches the slot date → `dateOverrideExist = true`
3. The `===` comparison on line 114 between two different dayjs objects is always false (object reference comparison), so it does not return true
4. `slotEndTime` (2:30 PM or 3:00 PM) is NOT before `date.start` (10:00 AM) → does not return true
5. `slotStartTime` (2:00 PM) is NOT after `date.end` (6:00 PM) → does not return true
6. The callback returns `undefined`, `find()` returns `undefined` (falsy)
7. The outer `if` block is skipped
8. `dateOverrideExist` is `true` → **`return true`** (slot marked as available)
9. The `busy.every()` check at line 153 is **never reached**
10. The 2:00 PM booking is ignored, and the slot is shown as bookable → **double booking**

## Impact

This bug affects every user who has date overrides configured. Any slot that falls within a date override window will always be shown as available, regardless of existing bookings. This can lead to double bookings, which is a serious scheduling integrity issue.

## Fix

Replace `return true` on line 134 with either removing the block entirely or letting execution fall through to the `busy.every()` check. The date override logic should only gate whether a slot is within the allowed time window — it should not bypass the busy-time conflict check. For example:

```diff
  if (dateOverrideExist) {
-   return true;
+   // Slot is within the date override window; still need to check busy times below
  }
```

Or restructure so that after confirming the slot is within the override, execution continues to the `busy.every()` check.

• Limited observability before destructive deletion: Terminal failures result in silent deletion with only console.log visibility—no structured metrics, reason codes, dead-letter tracking, or audit trail. **Order-sensitive `toEqual` on non-deterministically ordered arrays**

### Analysis
• **Service boundary erosion**: Removing the `findMany` method and replacing it with `getBaseConditions` exposes query composition to callers, pushing `$queryRaw` execution responsibility outside the service. This breaks encapsulation and differs from the parallel `InsightsRoutingService` pattern.

• **Inconsistent service layer APIs**: `InsightsRoutingService` maintains a `findMany` method that encapsulates data access, while `InsightsBookingService` now forces callers to handle raw query execution. This inconsistency creates a maintainability burden and makes services harder to compose or swap.

• **Type safety regression**: Switching from `Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedWhereInput` to raw `Prisma.sql` templates loses compile-time schema validation. While parameterization prevents SQL injection, typos in column names won't be caught until runtime.

• **Test brittleness**: Integration tests now validate exact SQL structure rather than query behavior, coupling them to implementation details and making them fragile to benign formatting changes.

Summary
- The PR converts InsightsBookingService internals and its integration tests from Prisma object-style where-clauses to raw Prisma.sql template literal conditions.
- Main changes: introduce NOTHING_CONDITION = Prisma.sql`1=0`, make authorization/filter builders return Prisma.Sql, add getBaseConditions(), update tests to compare Prisma.sql and to run an actual $queryRaw using the returned SQL fragment.
- Overall approach is consistent and the parameterization seems preserved by using Prisma.sql`... ${value}`.

What I looked for
- Correctness of logic translations (AND/OR structure preserved)
- Safety: parameter binding / SQL injection risks
- Edge cases: empty arrays (ANY), null/undefined conditions
- Test assertions reliability (comparing Prisma.sql objects)
- Type correctness and caching behavior

Findings and suggestions

1) Using Prisma.sql.join vs manual reduce
- You manually reduce SQL fragments to combine with AND/OR:
  return conditions.reduce((acc, condition, index) => { ... });
- Consider using Prisma.sql and Prisma.join for clarity and to avoid accidental parenthesis mistakes. Example:

  const joined = Prisma.sql`${Prisma.join(conditions.map(c => Prisma.sql`(${c})`), Prisma.sql` OR `)}`;
  return joined;

  Or for AND:
  Prisma.sql`${Prisma.join(conditions, Prisma.sql` AND `)}`

- This is cleaner and less error-prone than reduce.

2) ANY(...) with JS arrays — behavior & edge cases
- You use ("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})) and ("userId" = ANY(${uniqueUserIds})).
- Passing a JS array as ${teamIds} should be parameterized by Prisma -> Postgres array. That generally works (node-postgres converts arrays to SQL arrays).
- Edge case: ANY('{}') (empty array) yields false for all comparisons. You already avoid building the userId ANY clause when the array is empty, which is good.
- For teamIds you always include options.orgId, so teamIds won't be empty — fine.

3) NOTHINg condition: Prisma.sql`1=0`
- Using Prisma.sql`1=0` as NOTHING_CONDITION is fine for queries, but tests compare Prisma.sql objects directly (expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`)).
- Be aware: Prisma.sql returns an object with text/values; two separately created Prisma.sql template literals (even with the same contents) might not be ===, but Jest/Vitest toEqual compares deep equality of objects. The generated objects include identical structure so tests may pass, but it can be brittle.
- Recommendation: keep the NOTHING_CONDITION constant exported or reused by both service and tests (you already add a constant in tests), that's fine. Ensure any comparisons use the same construction semantics — or better, compare the serialized SQL and parameters:

  // Example assertion (more robust)
  expect(conditions.sql).toBeDefined();
  expect(String(conditions)).toContain('1=0');
  // or if the Prisma.Sql object has .query and .params, compare those.

4) getBaseConditions behavior and empty cases
- getBaseConditions returns:
  - combined (auth AND filter) if both present
  - single side if only one present
  - NOTHING_CONDITION if neither present
- This matches previous behavior where an impossible condition was returned on invalid inputs.
- Good: make sure callers (like the $queryRaw) always interpolate the returned Prisma.Sql directly as you do. Your $queryRaw uses WHERE ${baseConditions} which should parameterize correctly.

5) SQL quoting of column names
- You used double quotes around column names (e.g., "userId"). This matches Postgres naming; if your DB has those column names as camelCase in schema this is correct. If your Prisma mapping uses different underlying column names, ensure these match the DB actual names. Previously Prisma object-where would map correctly, but in raw SQL you must match DB columns. Confirm column names in BookingTimeStatusDenormalized match these quoted identifiers. If the database schema uses snake_case, the queries would break.

6) Parameterization / SQL injection
- All user-supplied values are interpolated via Prisma.sql`${value}` — that yields bound parameters; safe from SQL injection.
- Only caution: constructing SQL fragments by interpolating raw SQL strings (not values) would be unsafe. You're interpolating arrays/ids which are safe.

7) Tests: comparing Prisma.sql expressions
- Many tests assert equality against inline Prisma.sql template literals. Be cautious: if the service constructs the SQL in a slightly different parenthesis arrangement, deep equality may fail even if semantically equivalent.
- Instead of deep equality, consider:
  - Comparing the stringified SQL and the parameters (if accessible), or
  - Using a helper to normalize the SQL before comparing (strip extra parentheses/whitespace), or
  - Use Prisma.join in both implementation and tests to produce stable shapes.
- Example helper for tests:

  function sqlToString(s: Prisma.Sql) {
    // Prisma.Sql is an object with .text and .values in some implementations
    // Adapt depending on runtime shape
    return s?.toString?.() ?? JSON.stringify(s);
  }

  expect(sqlToString(conditions)).toContain('"userId" =');

8) Caching behavior
- You changed cachedAuthConditions/cachedFilterConditions types to Prisma.Sql which is correct.
- You lazily populate them when undefined — OK.
- Note: if options or filters change on the same instance after creation, cache won't refresh. That's likely intentional.

9) Small type / consistency nitpicks
- You added InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions with optional teamId; the constructor now accepts that and then validates via zod schema — good.
- In isOrgOwnerOrAdmin you replaced includes([...]) with explicit OR comparison; that's clearer and avoids creating arrays — fine.

10) Suggest adding a unit/integration test for an empty team/user list case
- E.g., team exists but no memberships -> verify OR branch doesn't include ANY(...) for empty arrays (you already handle that), but add explicit coverage.

11) Minor test expectation updates
- In the last integration test you switched to $queryRaw returning [{id}] and assert equals full array — good. Consider selecting more fields in case of duplicates.

Summary of recommended changes
- Prefer Prisma.join to combine SQL fragments rather than manual reduce.

🔴 SQL operator precedence bug: `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` produce top-level OR expressions without outer parentheses. When `getBaseConditions()` returns these directly (line 75, no filters), callers composing with AND (e.g., `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND createdAt > date`) get incorrect precedence — AND binds tighter than OR, so team bookings bypass additional filters entirely. Fix: wrap the return at line 75 with parens around authConditions, or add outer parens in the reduce calls. Additionally, since `authConditions` is always a `Prisma.Sql` object (never null), the `else if (filterConditions)` and `else` branches (lines 76-80) are unreachable dead code.

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## What the bug is

`buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` (line 171-174) and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` (line 204-207) use `reduce` to join conditions with OR:

```typescript
return conditions.reduce((acc, condition, index) => {
  if (index === 0) return condition;
  return Prisma.sql`(${acc}) OR (${condition})`;
});
```

With two conditions, this produces: `(team_cond) OR (user_cond)`. Note the outer parens only wrap `acc` (the left side from the previous iteration), not the entire expression. The top-level OR has no enclosing parentheses.

## How it triggers

When `getBaseConditions()` is called for org or team scope WITHOUT filter conditions, the `else if (authConditions)` branch at line 74-75 returns `authConditions` directly — unwrapped. A caller composing this with additional AND conditions (the standard pattern for insights queries, e.g. date ranges) would produce:

```sql
WHERE (("teamId" = ANY([1,2,3])) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true))
  OR (("userId" = ANY([4,5,6])) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false))
  AND "createdAt" > '2024-01-01'
```

Due to SQL operator precedence (AND binds tighter than OR), this is parsed as:

```sql
WHERE (("teamId" = ANY([1,2,3])) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true))
  OR ((("userId" = ANY([4,5,6])) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false)) AND "createdAt" > '2024-01-01')
```

The team bookings condition is NOT filtered by the date range — ALL team bookings are returned regardless.

## Step-by-step proof

1. Create an `InsightsBookingService` with `scope: "team"`, no filters.
2. `getBaseConditions()` calls `getAuthorizationConditions()` which calls `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition()`.
3. `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition()` returns: `(("teamId" = 5) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)) OR (("userId" = ANY([10,11])) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false))` — no outer parens around the whole expression.
4. `getFilterConditions()` returns `null` (no filters).
5. `getBaseConditions()` enters the `else if (authConditions)` branch (line 74) and returns the auth conditions raw.
6. A caller writes: `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "createdAt" > '2024-01-01'`
7. The resulting SQL has AND binding tighter than OR, so the date filter only applies to the user-bookings branch. All team bookings are returned unfiltered.

## Contrast with the correct path

When BOTH auth and filter conditions exist, line 72-73 wraps them correctly: `(${authConditions}) AND (${filterConditions})`. The outer parens around `authConditions` prevent the precedence issue. Only the "auth only" path at line 75 is missing this protection.

## Impact

This is a data correctness and potential authorization issue. For org/team scope queries without filters, callers would receive unfiltered team bookings, potentially exposing data outside the intended date range or other constraints.

## Dead code (minor)

Since `getAuthorizationConditions()` returns `Promise<Prisma.Sql>` (never null/undefined), `authConditions` is always a truthy `Prisma.Sql` object. The `else if (filterConditions)` branch (line 76-77) and the `else` branch with `NOTHING_CONDITION` (lines 78-80) are unreachable dead code. This isn't functionally broken — the first two branches handle all cases correctly — but it's misleading code that suggests auth conditions could be absent when they cannot be. One refutation correctly notes this is "not functionally wrong" — agreed, it's a nit-level readability issue, but worth simplifying alongside the main fix.

## How to fix

Either:
- Wrap the return at line 75: `return Prisma.sql(${authConditions})`
- Or wrap the final OR reduction in `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` and `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` with outer parens

The first approach is simpler and also protects against future changes to the auth condition builders. Optionally, simplify the dead branches to just two branches (auth+filter vs auth-only).

</details>

🟡 Nit: The constructor parameter type was changed from `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` (discriminated union requiring `teamId` when `scope: "team"`) to `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` (flat type with `teamId?: number`), which loses compile-time enforcement that `teamId` is provided for team scope. While runtime zod validation catches this (returning `NOTHING_CONDITION`), the failure mode is silent empty results instead of a compile error. Consider keeping `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` as the constructor param type for consistency with `InsightsRoutingService` (insightsRouting.ts:52).

<details>
<summary>Extended reasoning...</summary>

## What the bug is

The PR introduces a new type `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` at line 28-33 of `insightsBooking.ts` that defines `teamId` as optional (`teamId?: number`) across all scopes. The constructor parameter type was changed from `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` (the zod-inferred discriminated union) to this new looser type. The discriminated union correctly requires `teamId: z.number()` only when `scope` is `"team"` (line 23-26), providing compile-time safety.

## How it manifests

With the new `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` type, a caller can write:
```typescript
new InsightsBookingService({
  prisma,
  options: { scope: "team", userId: 1, orgId: 1 },  // missing teamId - no TypeScript error!
});
```
TypeScript will not flag this as an error. The runtime zod `safeParse` at line 63 catches the invalid input and sets `this.options` to `null`, which causes `buildAuthorizationConditions()` to return `NOTHING_CONDITION` (`1=0`). This means queries silently return zero results instead of failing at compile time.

## Why existing code does not prevent it

The zod schema validation does catch the issue at runtime, but this converts a compile-time error into a silent runtime failure. The `safeParse` approach is intentional for the boundary validation, but the constructor type should still be strict to catch mistakes during development. The fact that invalid options result in `null` (and then `NOTHING_CONDITION`) means the failure is secure but completely silent - no error is logged or thrown.

## Inconsistency with InsightsRoutingService

The sibling service `InsightsRoutingService` at `insightsRouting.ts:52` still uses its strict discriminated union type (`InsightsRoutingServiceOptions`) as the constructor parameter. This creates an inconsistency within the codebase - one insights service enforces `teamId` at compile time for team scope, the other does not.

## Impact and addressing the intentional design counterargument

One could argue the `PublicOptions` type is intentionally looser for API boundaries. However, the `InsightsRoutingService` - the sibling service following the same pattern - still uses the strict discriminated union. If this were an intentional pattern, both services should follow it. The impact is limited since: (1) no production callers exist yet, (2) the runtime validation prevents security issues (returns no data rather than too much data), and (3) the fix is trivial. However, as more callers are added, the lack of compile-time enforcement could lead to subtle bugs where team-scoped queries silently return empty results.

## Suggested fix

Keep `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` (the discriminated union) as the constructor parameter type instead of `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`. The runtime `safeParse` can remain as defense-in-depth, but the constructor signature should enforce the correct shape at compile time, matching the pattern used in `InsightsRoutingService`.

</details>

P3: Public methods `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` return `Prisma.Sql` fragments containing OR operators without outer parentheses. For example, `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` returns `(teamCondition) OR (userCondition)` and `buildFilterConditions` with only eventTypeId returns `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)`. While `getBaseConditions()` wraps these in parens correctly, any caller that composes these public methods directly into a raw query with AND (e.g., `Prisma.sql\`${authConditions} AND "startTime" > ${date}\``) would hit SQL operator precedence bugs: AND binds tighter than OR, so one branch of the OR would bypass the AND condition. For auth conditions this would be a privilege escalation (org team bookings returned without date filter). The fix is to wrap the final return value of each builder in outer parentheses.

In some cases (`googlecalendar`, `hubspot`, `zohocrm`, `zoho-bigin`), `refreshFunction` returns an object with a `data` property (like an Axios response) or the data directly, while the calling code expects this structure. However, the `fetch` path returns a `Response` object, which will break the calling code (e.g., `res?.data` will be undefined). In other cases (`larkcalendar`, `office365calendar`, etc.), the `refreshFunction` returns a `Response` object, and the calling code is prepared to handle it. This inconsistency will lead to runtime errors. You should decide on a single return contract for `refreshOAuthTokens` and adapt all call sites and `refreshFunction` implementations accordingly. For example, it could always return the parsed JSON data.

The schema `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is too broad. The line `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` will match *any* property with a number value and treat it as an expiry time.
